name: Precautionary in case

1.definition: Supplies the possibility against which the main action is a precaution.

examples.form: Take a key [in case the door locks].

projection.target: The taking is appropriate before it is known whether the door will lock. An if-adjunct can instead make taking conditional on the door locking.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Doing something just in case
curious.summary: A phrase beginning with in case names a possibility that you're guarding against, so the main action is a precaution.
curious.body: In Take a key in case the door locks, the part after in case names a possibility. The taking happens as a precaution against it. You don't need to know yet whether the door will lock. That makes it different from a version with if. Take a key if the door locks makes the taking depend on the door locking. With in case, the taking is appropriate before anyone knows how things will turn out.

examples.text: Take a key [in case the door locks].
Pack a coat [in case it rains].

curious.try: Compare Take a key in case the door locks with Take a key if the door locks. When would you pick up the key in each one?

teacher.summary: Useful for learners who treat in case as interchangeable with if.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a prepositional phrase made of in case plus a finite clause. It supplies the possibility against which the main action is a precaution. The main action is appropriate before it is known whether the possibility will come about. An if-adjunct can instead make the main action conditional on that possibility. So the two forms invite different readings of the same main clause, as in Take a key in case the door locks versus Take a key if the door locks. The dictionary marks this dictionary as provisional and relates it to the general prepositional phrase and to if-conditionals.
teacher.terms: Sometimes described as a precautionary or contingency use of in case. The if version is a conditional adjunct.

examples.text: Take a key [in case the door locks].
Bring an umbrella [in case it rains].

contrasts.text: Take a key in case the door locks.
contrasts.note: Precaution; taken before it's known whether the door will lock.

contrasts.text: Take a key if the door locks.
contrasts.note: Taking depends on the door locking.

watch_for: A learner might treat in case and if as having the same meaning in Take a key in case the door locks.
A learner might think the in case clause describes something that has already happened.
teacher.activity: Give pairs of sentences that differ only in in case and if. Students say what you would do, and when, in each version, then write their own pair.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Precautionary in case." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/in-case-contingency-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).
